profile.address: County Road 10.7 Northwest, Quincy, Grant County, Washington
profile.reading:
This facility, NTT Data Quincy, is a legacy asset of NTT DATA's enterprise IT-services business rather than NTT's RagingWire-branded colocation arm, which explains why it does not appear on NTT Global Data Centers' current US locations page. The building was constructed by Dell in 2012 in Quincy, Grant County, Washington, a rural Columbia Basin town that became a data center hub in the 2000s for its cheap, abundant hydroelectric power. NTT DATA acquired the facility in 2016 as part of its roughly $3.05 billion purchase of Dell's Perot Systems/Dell Services IT-outsourcing division, according to Data Center Dynamics' reporting on the deal. On January 29, 2019, real estate investor GI Partners acquired the Quincy facility, along with NTT DATA's Plano, Texas headquarters campus, in a sale-leaseback transaction, with NTT DATA remaining as the long-term tenant and operator; GI Partners' own announcement describes the Quincy building as roughly 180,000 square feet with 14 megawatts of gross utility power, powered entirely by hydroelectric generation. A secondary aggregator source lists the facility's street address as 525 D St NW, Quincy, WA, which this entry notes as unconfirmed against a primary NTT or GI Partners filing.

Grant County's public utility district has built one of the country's most data-center-friendly rate structures around its Columbia and Priest Rapids hydroelectric dams, drawing Microsoft, Yahoo, and Sabey alongside NTT DATA to the Quincy area over the past two decades, making this one of the older, more established rural data center clusters tracked in this registry rather than a newer hyperscale build.

NTT's US Global Data Centers footprint spans seven named campuses in total: Ashburn, Virginia at 224 megawatts; Chicago, Illinois at more than 200 megawatts; Dallas, Texas at 160 megawatts; Hillsboro, Oregon at 126 megawatts; Phoenix, Arizona at 240 megawatts; and a combined Sacramento/Santa Clara, California figure of 68 megawatts, totaling roughly 1,118 megawatts or more of disclosed US capacity, per the operator's own locations page. The US business operates under the NTT DATA Global Data Centers Americas name, the successor brand to RagingWire Data Centers, now under Japan's NTT DATA Group and parent Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation, a Tokyo Stock Exchange-listed company not subject to SEC 10-K filing requirements.

reading.body:
NTT Data Quincy sits in Grant County, Washington, but publishes no power capacity figure for the campus. The facility ranks third among Washington state's data centers with published capacity, behind only two others that together account for 60 megawatts of stated IT load. This rank reflects the site's importance in the operator's US footprint, not a disclosed number.

Washington state has 46 mapped data center facilities, of which only three publish power figures at all. NTT Data Quincy's omission of a capacity spec places it among the vast majority of US campuses that do not disclose their scale to the public. The state context provides no grid information, transmission constraints, or power availability figures that would indicate whether Grant County's grid can support further AI buildout here.

The operator NTT is a top-tier global IT services and telecommunications firm with significant data center operations worldwide, but the specific capabilities, age, cooling systems, and electrical design of this campus are not published. No certifications, planned expansion, or current tenant commitments appear in available sources.
